Prescribing every singular direction

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Closedness and positive conicity are the only restrictions on the wavefront set of a complex distribution. We prove this in a form that realizes the same set simultaneously for smooth, analytic and every admissible derivative-growth regularity. The construction places singularities at a dense collection of base-direction pairs. A geometric gap gives holomorphic continuation everywhere else, while a strict coefficient bound prevents the chosen singularities from cancelling.

The prerequisites are Continuing the spherical kernel, Theorem 4 for the continuation domain, Theorem 6 for conic exponential decay, and Theorem 7 for positivity and boundary growth; Holomorphic decompositions of tempered distributions, Theorem 4 for its polynomial-growth converse; and Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Theorem 3 and Exercise 5 for the exact boundary characterization and restriction to open sets. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 3 and 5–7, supplies controlled localization, projection, comparison and finite sums. Polydisk Cauchy estimates and power series are proved in Section 3 of Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones. The Fourier foundation, F1–F5, fixes the transform and conjugation conventions, and the metric foundation supplies Euclidean compactness and the elementary topology used below.

Dense data and coefficients that cannot cancel

A cone is invariant under multiplication of its covector by every positive number. Let be a closed conic subset of , and write

It is closed in the unit-direction space. Suppose initially that it is nonempty. Choose distinct pairs , indexed either by or by all positive integers, whose set is dense in . Here is the elementary selection argument. Rational numbers are countable by listing their integer numerators and positive denominators in finite boxes of increasing size; finite tuples are countable by the same finite-box enumeration. Thus ambient rational-center, positive rational-radius balls are countable. They form a base: inside any open ball about a point, choose a rational center sufficiently close to that point, then a positive rational radius larger than that distance but small enough that the new ball remains inside the original ball. Density of the rationals is proved in Section 12 of the metric foundation. Intersecting these balls with the unit-direction space gives its countable base. Select a point from every such ball meeting , using the countable choice in the foundational assumptions, and remove repetitions. Every relative neighborhood contains one of these basis sets and therefore a selected point. If only finitely many distinct points result, keep that finite list. No infinite list without repetitions is required for a finite set.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — empty, finite and dense sets (foundation). Explain why the construction must allow a finite list of distinct pairs. For a finite nonempty , check the proof of Theorem 5 without adding repeated pairs. What distribution realizes the empty set?

Solution. A dense subset of a finite set must be that entire finite set: each of its points has a small ball avoiding the others. There is no infinite sequence of distinct points in it. Enumerate those points once and use the finite sum (7). The coefficient bounds (6) remain valid, because a finite tail is no larger than the infinite geometric tail. Earlier terms in Lemma 3 are still finite, and Lemma 4 applies unchanged (or directly by a finite intersection of continuation neighborhoods). Thus every selected singularity remains and there are no others. For the empty set, the zero distribution has identically zero localized transforms and realizes it in every class.

Exercise 2 — how much coefficient separation is needed? (intermediate). Replace by nonzero complex coefficients . Prove the same realization if and, for one , for every . Apply this to with arbitrary real phases and . What does the argument say at ?

Solution. In Lemmas 2 and 4, replace coefficient sums by sums of absolute values. Uniform convergence and holomorphic continuation are unchanged. At the -th pair the own term has magnitude , even when its phase is nonzero; the later tail has magnitude at most . The lower bound is therefore , which diverges. Theorem 5 follows as before. For the infinite geometric sequence the tail-to-term ratio is exactly ; finite tails are smaller. At this estimate has ratio one in the infinite case and supplies no positive divergent lower bound. It does not prove that cancellation must occur, only that this particular sufficient estimate no longer establishes absence of cancellation.

Exercise 3 — why complex distributions are allowed (advanced). Define . Prove

for or any . Deduce that a real distribution must have reflection-symmetric wavefront. If is symmetric and is supplied by Theorem 5, show that the union of the wavefronts of and is exactly , simultaneously in every class.

Solution. For a compact distribution, the definition of its Fourier transform gives , with a real cutoff equal to one near its support in the pairing. Conjugation preserves support and the finite-order bound. Conjugating an -witness sequence therefore gives a witness for on the reflected cone with exactly the same constants. Conjugating a second time gives the reverse implication and proves (22). For smooth wavefront, conjugate the compact cutoff witness as well; its conjugate is still one near the base point, and the same transform identity proves (22). If , the reflection symmetry follows. Thus a single positive ray over a point cannot be the wavefront of a real distribution.

When is symmetric, (22) gives . The finite-sum rule applied to and puts each of their wavefronts in . Applying the same rule to gives the opposite inclusion into their union. Both components are real distributions by the definition of conjugation. This proves the union statement; it does not assert that either component alone has every prescribed singularity.

Exercise 4 — accumulation at the boundary of an open set (advanced). On , prescribe only positive covectors over the points , . Prove that this is a valid relatively closed conic set and compute its closure in the full punctured cotangent space. Explain the role of restriction in Theorem 5.

Solution. The only accumulation point of these base points outside the set itself is zero. One proof is that any sequence of distinct indices tends to infinity along a subsequence, forcing the reciprocal subsequence to tend to zero; bounded indices supply only finitely many values. Zero is outside , so the set of base points is closed relative to . The positive direction is a closed component of . Their product is therefore relatively closed and conic. Its full closure adds precisely the positive ray over zero, because convergence in the punctured cotangent space has a nonzero limiting covector and cannot change its positive sign. The global construction realizes this enlarged set. Restricting to removes its fiber over zero and gives exactly the prescribed local set. No unwanted negative direction or base point is introduced.

Exercise 5 — independently choosing the two one-dimensional signs (intermediate). Let be any two relatively closed subsets of an open . Construct a distribution whose singular directions are positive exactly over and negative exactly over , simultaneously for every class in (16). Identify its smooth and analytic singular supports.

Solution. The set is relatively closed in the punctured cotangent space: each sign component is open and closed there, and each base set is relatively closed in . It is conic. Apply Theorem 5. Its projection to the base is . The analytic projection theorem proved in the conic lesson identifies this with analytic singular support. Outside the union the distribution is analytic, hence smooth. At any point of the union at least one smooth wavefront direction is present by (16), whereas a smooth function has no such direction by the compact-cutoff integration-by-parts estimate. Thus its smooth singular support is also precisely . In particular the two regularity singular supports coincide for this construction even when the individual positive and negative direction sets differ.
